question: How do I find peace when everything around me is chaotic?
answer: Peace begins within, not by changing the chaos around you. When you steady your mind through self-control and reason—letting go of attachment to outcomes and sensory distractions—you remain unmoved by external turmoil, as BG-6.7 and BG-18.51 teach. Start by pausing each day to observe your breath without judgment, noticing when you react to noise or stress, and gently returning your attention inward. What small moment of stillness could you claim for yourself today?
cited_verses:
[BG-6.7] The Self of one who is self-controlled and has attained peace is equally unmoved by heat or cold, pleasure or pain, honor or dishonor.

[BG-18.51] Guided always by pure reason, bravely restraining himself, renouncing the objects of sense and giving up attachment and hatred; he attains peace.

question: Should I quit my stable job to join a startup?
answer: Before making a leap, see if your current role lets you act with clarity and purpose—confusion often grows when leaders become distant or delay decisions. AS-1.19.7 warns that inaccessibility breeds disorder, while AS-3.14.1 reminds us that work entrusted must be met with timely effort, whether by you or a capable substitute. Ask yourself: will the startup give you the agency to act decisively, or risk leaving you waiting at the door? What’s one small step you could take this week to test that?
cited_verses:
[AS-1.19.7] When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.

[AS-3.14.1] A servant neglecting or unreasonably putting off work for which he has received wages shall be fined 12 panas and be caught-hold of till the work is done. He who is incapable to turn out work, or is engaged to do a mean job, or is suffering from disease, or is involved in calamities shall be shown some concession or allowed to get the work done by a substitute. The loss incurred by his master or employer owing to such delay shall be made good by extra work.
note: AS-1.19.7 is about a king being accessible to petitioners and AS-3.14.1 about fining neglectful servants; stretched onto a career decision. Does not help weigh the startup choice.

question: How do I audit the people who handle money in my organisation?
answer: Start by making sure your financial oversight is part of regular work, not an afterthought. AS-2.6.12 reminds us that auditing revenue is core to good governance—so build checks into daily routines, not just occasional reviews. When people handle money, clarity and access matter: AS-1.19.7 warns that leaders who distance themselves breed confusion and risk—stay approachable so issues surface early. Consider too that those who spot problems deserve recognition; AS-2.8.21 shows rewarding honesty strengthens integrity. How might you weave these ideas into your team’s current practices?
cited_verses:
[AS-2.6.12] The business of upkeeping the government (samsthánam), the routine work (prachárah), the collection of necessaries of life, the collection and audit of all kinds of revenue,—these constitute the work in hand.

[AS-1.19.7] When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.

[AS-2.8.21] Any informant (súchaka) who supplies information about embezzlement just under perpetration shall, if he succeeds in proving it, get as reward one-sixth of the amount in question; if he happens to be a government servant (bhritaka), he shall get for the same act one-twelfth of the amount.
note: AS-2.6.12 and AS-2.8.21 fit; AS-1.19.7 (leader accessibility) is stretched to auditing.

question: How should a ruler divide and organise his working day?
answer: Structure your day so you are accessible to those who need you, not locked away with advisors. AS-1.19.7 warns that making yourself unavailable breeds confusion and weakens your position. Stay present, delegate wisely, and keep your work transparent. How does that fit the rhythm of your current responsibilities?
cited_verses: [AS-1.19.7] When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.
note: Cites only AS-1.19.7 (accessibility); the verse on dividing the day (AS-1.19.3) is not cited. Advice "delegate, stay transparent" is not in the verse.

question: I keep chasing success but I never feel satisfied
answer:
You’re running after success yet still feel empty inside—this is exactly what Arjuna confessed when he said he never felt satisfied listening to divine words.

The Gita reminds you that true contentment comes not from chasing results but from acting with your mind steady, free from attachment to success or failure (BG-2.48). It also urges you to look inward, letting your higher self guide you rather than letting disappointment drag you down (BG-6.5).

What’s one small action you could take today not for the outcome, but simply because it aligns with who you truly are?
cited_verses:
[BG-2.48] Perform all your actions with your mind concentrated on the Divine, renouncing attachment and looking upon success and failure with an equal eye. Spirituality implies equanimity.

[BG-6.5] Let him seek liberation with the help of his Highest Self, and never disgrace his own Self. For that Self is his only friend; yet it can also be his enemy.
note: Opens with a claim that Arjuna "confessed he never felt satisfied listening to divine words": that is BG-10.18 (uncited), and it is about wanting to hear more, not restless chasing. Also assumes "feel empty".

question: I am jealous of my friends who are doing better than me
answer: Jealousy steals your peace when you measure yourself against others. BG-12.18 reminds you to see friend and foe alike, not letting their success shake your inner steadiness. BG-14.25 points to the freedom that comes when honor and dishonor, gain and loss, feel equal to you. What small step could you take today to shift your focus from their path to your own?
cited_verses:
[BG-12.18] He to whom friend and foe are alike, who welcomes equally honor and dishonor, heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and who is enamored of nothing—

[BG-14.25] Who looks equally upon honor and dishonor, loves friends and foes alike, and abandons all initiative, such is he who transcends the qualities.
note: 12.18/14.25 are about equanimity to honor/dishonor; "gain and loss" is not in 14.25. Does not really address jealousy.

question: mujhe lagta hai sab kuch meri galti hai, I can't focus on anything
answer: Tumhare dil ki baat samajh mein aati hoon—lagta hai har cheez pe tumhe khud se gussa hai, aur wajah yeh ki focus nahi ho raha. BG-2.62 kehte hain ki jab hum kisi baat par zyada sochte hain, to usse attachment badhta hai, phir frustration aati hai. BG-7.28 kehte hain ki jab mann se dwaandva moh hat jaye, to woh shanti se kaam kar sakta hai. Tumhein kya lagta hai ki ab ek chhota sa kaam karke dekhna sahi rahega?
cited_verses:
[BG-2.62] When a person dwells on the objects of sense, they create an attraction for them; this attraction develops into desire, and desire breeds anger.

[BG-7.28] But those who act righteously, in whom sin has been destroyed, who are free from the infatuation of conflicting emotions, they worship Me with a firm resolve.
note: Assumes anger at oneself, which the user did not say; does not address the self-blame. 7.28 paraphrase adds "shanti". Hinglish register is appropriate.

question: How do I detect and handle a conspiracy inside my own camp?
answer: First, notice the quiet signs—shifting loyalties, whispered doubts, or someone pushing their own gain over the team’s purpose. AS-9.3.12 teaches that when someone of good intent conspires for shared benefit, seek agreement; but when their temper is obstinate, let them reveal their hand, then respond with clarity. AS-12.3.2 adds that trusted voices can gently expose hidden agendas by framing concerns as the leader’s own stance, not accusation. Watch who benefits from confusion, and who avoids direct talk. What small step could you take this week to test where true alignment lies?
cited_verses:
[AS-9.3.12] When a person of good disposition makes a conspiracy for the purpose of acquiring what is to be enjoyed by both then an agreement should be made with him. But when a person of obstinate temper so conspires, he should be allowed to have his own way and then deceived. Thus the form of policy to be adopted should be considered.

[AS-12.3.2] Spies may also tell those who have not received what they requested of the king (the enemy) that the officer in charge of waste lands has been told by the king: "Such and such a person has begged of me what he should not demand; I refused to grant his request; he is in conspiracy with my enemy. So make attempts to put him down." Then the spies may proceed in their usual way.
note: AS-9.3.12 says the obstinate conspirator is allowed his way and then deceived; the answer softens this to "reveal his hand". AS-12.3.2 is spies falsely branding someone a conspirator; the answer recasts it as gentle exposure. Sanitises/misrepresents both.

question: papa chahte hain main unka business sambhalun but mera mann nahi hai
answer: Tumhare mann ki awaz sunna zaroori hai – koi kaam dil se na ho to usme safalta mushkil hoti hai. AS-8.1.3 ke mutabik, kisi bhi kaam ka sahi anujami minister ya sahayogi ki madad se hi possible hai; agar tumhare andar ichha nahi, to business sambhalna buri tarah se ho sakta hai. Papa ki ummeed samajhna bhi important hai, lekhna ki tum dono ki baat samjhein aur ek aisa rasta nikale jo dono ke liye theek ho. Kya tum ek baar baith kar papa se khul kar baat kar sakte ho ki tumhein kya lagta hai?
cited_verses: [AS-8.1.3] No, says Bháradvája, of the distress of the king and of his minister, ministerial distress is more serious; deliberations in council, the attainment of results as anticipated while deliberating in council, the accomplishment of works, the business of revenue-collection and its expenditure, recruiting the army, the driving out of the enemy and of wild tribes, the protection of the kingdom, taking remedial measures against calamities, the protection of the heir-apparent, and the installation of princes constitute the duties of ministers. In the absence of ministers; the above works are ill-done; and like a bird, deprived of its feathers, the king loses his active capacity. In such calamities, the intrigues of the enemy find a ready scope. In ministerial distress, the king's life itself comes into danger, for a minister is the mainstay of the security of the king's life.
note: AS-8.1.3 is about ministerial distress; the claim that work succeeds only with ministers/helpers and fails without desire is not in the verse. The advice to talk with the father is sound but not from the verse.

answer:
The part you can act on is your own conduct and effort in the next step, not the outcome that follows it.

answer: Exam ki tension se neend udd jaane lagti hai, yaar. question: I am working sixteen hours a day and I am burnt out
answer: You’re stretched thin and it’s wearing you down—no one can sustain sixteen-hour days without cost. AS-3.14.1 reminds us that when work overwhelms capacity, concession or substitution is due, not punishment. AS-8.5.1 names exhaustion and displeasure from disappointment as real troubles that sap strength, just as you’re feeling. What’s one small task you could hand off or pause this week to protect your energy?

question: How should punishment be applied so it is neither too harsh nor too lenient?
answer: Punishment should fit the act, not the mood of the one giving it—neither born of anger nor of indifference, but of clear judgment that sees what is truly due. When you act without liking or disliking the outcome, focused only on what is right in the moment, your response naturally avoids excess or lack (BG-18.23). This inner steadiness lets you apply correction as deserved, which earns respect rather than fear or contempt (AS-1.4.5). What is one small situation coming up where you can pause, check your motive, and act only because it is right?
cited_verses:
[BG-18.23] An obligatory action done by one who is disinterested, who neither likes nor dislikes it, and gives no thought to the consequences that may follow, such an action is Pure.

[AS-1.4.5] "No," says Kautilya; for whoever imposes severe punishment becomes repulsive to the people; while he who awards mild punishment becomes contemptible. But whoever imposes punishment as deserved becomes respectable. For punishment (danda) when awarded with due consideration, makes the people devoted to righteousness and to works productive of wealth and enjoyment; while punishment, when ill-awarded under the influence of greed and anger or owing to ignorance, excites fury even among hermits and ascetics dwelling in forests, not to speak of householders.
note: BG-18.23 applied to the judge's motive is a reasonable link; AS-1.4.5 accurate.

question: My parents want me to marry someone I do not love
answer: You're caught between your parents' wishes and your own heart. BG-2.62 shows how dwelling on what others want can stir desire that turns into inner conflict when it doesn't match your truth. BG-15.5 reminds us that peace comes when we release attachment to external expectations and connect with what is genuine within. What small step could you take this week to honor your own feelings while staying open to dialogue?

[BG-2.62] When a person dwells on the objects of sense, they create an attraction for them; this attraction develops into desire, and desire breeds anger.

question: I hate myself for the mistakes I have made
answer: You're carrying a heavy weight of self-blame right now, and it's okay to feel that sting of regret. BG-2.63 reminds us that anger—especially toward ourselves—clouds judgment and keeps us stuck in cycles of pain. BG-5.28 points toward freedom that comes when we gently govern our mind and heart, not with harshness, but with steady, kind attention. What small step could you take today to treat yourself with the same patience you'd offer a friend?

note: BG-2.63 read as self-directed anger is a stretch; BG-5.28 fine. Warm and non-preachy.

question: My wife and I keep arguing about money
answer: Money arguments often start with small frustrations that grow when we feel unheard or unfairly treated. AS-4.7.17 reminds us that anger over money or perceived slights can damage what matters most—so pause before reacting, and ask yourself what you’re really trying to protect. AS-3.2.11 shows how property and resources are tied to care and responsibility, not just ownership—think about what your wife might need to feel secure, not just what’s being spent. Try talking when you’re both calm, not in the heat of the moment, and listen to understand her worry before explaining yours. What’s one small thing you could do this week to show her you’re on her side, even when you disagree?
cited_verses:
[AS-4.7.17] Offence to women or kinsmen, claiming inheritance, professional competition, hatred against rivals, commerce, guilds and any one of the legal disputes, is the cause of anger: anger is the cause of death.

If there are no sons, her daughters shall have it. question: Nothing I do seems to matter. What is the point of any of this?
answer: Your feeling that nothing matters is real, and it's okay to sit with that heaviness for a moment. When actions feel futile, it often comes from being caught in cycles of desire or frustration that cloud our sense of purpose, as BG-2.62 describes how dwelling on sensory pursuits fuels attachment, desire, and then anger—a loop that can make effort feel pointless. BG-7.28 offers a different path: acting righteously, free from inner conflict, allows us to engage with life from a place of steady resolve, not outcome. What small action could you take today that aligns with what feels right, regardless of whether it "matters" in the big picture?
cited_verses:
[BG-2.62] When a person dwells on the objects of sense, they create an attraction for them; this attraction develops into desire, and desire breeds anger.

[BG-7.28] But those who act righteously, in whom sin has been destroyed, who are free from the infatuation of conflicting emotions, they worship Me with a firm resolve.
note: Verses (sense attachment, righteous action) do not speak to meaninglessness; kind tone. No safety concern in the question.

question: My father passed away last month and I cannot stop crying
answer: I hear how deeply you're missing your father, and it's natural for tears to come when love runs this deep. The Gita reminds us that the wise do not grieve for those who have passed, for the soul is eternal (BG-2.11). Your father's love remains with you, not in the body but in the bond that death cannot break. What small thing could you do today that would honor his memory?
cited_verses: [BG-2.11] Lord Shri Krishna said: Why grieve for those for whom no grief is due, yet professing wisdom? The wise grieve neither for the dead nor the living.
note: BG-2.11 is a rebuke to grief ("why grieve"); the answer adds "soul is eternal" and "bond that death cannot break", which are not in the verse. Warm, but "the wise do not grieve" risks sounding dismissive.

question: Should I take a job that pays more but bores me?
answer: You’re weighing higher pay against feeling bored—a real trade-off many face when work no longer engages you. AS-3.14.1 reminds us that taking wages for work we neglect or delay unfairly harms both employer and self; staying in a role that bores you risks becoming that neglectful servant, owing effort you can’t genuinely give. AS-2.7.2 highlights tracking profit, loss, and effort—here, the “loss” is your disengagement, which over time drains your energy and growth more than extra pay compensates. Before deciding, ask: can you find meaning or negotiate new challenges in this role, or would honesty now serve you both better? What small step could you take this week to test whether the boredom is fixable or a sign to move on?

[AS-3.14.1] A servant neglecting or unreasonably putting off work for which he has received wages shall be fined 12 panas and be caught-hold of till the work is done. The loss incurred by his master or employer owing to such delay shall be made good by extra work.

question: How do I gather reliable information about what is really happening?
answer: Start by grounding your search in inner clarity—let go of fear and desire so your inquiry stays steady and true, as BG-5.28 teaches. Then, like a careful observer noting what unfolds in fields and markets, gather facts plainly without twisting them to fit hopes or fears, echoing the discreet, purposeful watchfulness of AS-2.35.13. What small step will you take today to listen more closely to what is actually said and done?

question: I feel restless and my mind never settles
answer: Your restless mind is asking for a moment of peace, and that’s a natural longing. When you gently turn your attention inward—whether through quiet breath, a simple mantra, or just watching thoughts pass—you begin to steady the wandering mind, as BG-8.8 reminds us that focused meditation leads to inner stillness. Likewise, BG-2.48 teaches that performing even small actions with a calm, unattached heart brings equanimity, helping the mind settle over time. What’s one tiny pause you could invite into your day today, just to notice your breath or a single sensation?
cited_verses:
[BG-8.8] He whose mind does not wander, and who is engaged in constant meditation, attains the Supreme Spirit.

[BG-2.48] Perform all your actions with your mind concentrated on the Divine, renouncing attachment and looking upon success and failure with an equal eye. Spirituality implies equanimity.

question: I feel alone even when I am surrounded by people
answer: Loneliness in a crowd often means your heart is seeking a deeper connection than the moment offers. BG-13.11 points to finding solace in turning inward, loving the quiet where you can meet yourself without distraction. BG-9.22 reminds that steady attention to what gives your life meaning brings a quiet assurance that you are not truly abandoned. What small practice helps you feel that inner steadiness when the noise around you feels empty?
cited_verses:
[BG-13.11] Unswerving devotion to Me, with concentration on Me and Me alone, a love for solitude, and indifference to social life;

[BG-9.22] But if a person meditates on Me and Me alone, worships Me always and everywhere, I will take upon Myself the fulfillment of their aspiration, and I will safeguard whatever they attain.
note: BG-13.11 endorses solitude and indifference to social life, which sits oddly with someone who feels alone; no encouragement to connect with people.

question: When should I make peace with a rival instead of fighting?
answer:
Make peace when you're not strong enough to win or when both sides are equally matched and open to it—wisdom lies in choosing the path that preserves your strength and opens room for future resolution.

In your situation, if your rival holds more power or if fighting would drain you without clear gain, seeking peace isn't surrender—it's strategy, as when the weaker seeks protection or equal terms (AS-7.1.5, AS-7.2.5). If you're evenly matched and they're willing to talk, that too is a moment for peace, not prolonged conflict (AS-7.1.8, AS-10.3.20).

What’s one small step you could take today to test whether peace is possible—perhaps a quiet message or a neutral meeting ground?
cited_verses:
[AS-7.1.5] Whoever is inferior to another shall make peace with him; whoever is superior in power shall wage war; whoever thinks "no enemy can hurt me, nor am I strong enough to destroy my enemy," shall observe neutrality; whoever is possessed of necessary means shall march against his enemy; whoever is devoid of necessary strength to defend himself shall seek the protection of another; whoever thinks that help is necessary to work out an end shall make peace with one and wage war with another. Such is the aspect of the six forms of policy.

[AS-7.2.5] A king who is situated between two powerful kings shall seek protection from the stronger of the two; or from one of them on whom he can rely; or he may make peace with both of them on equal terms. Then he may begin to set one of them against the other by telling each that the other is a tyrant causing utter ruin to himself, and thus cause dissension between them. When they are divided, he may pat down each separately by secret or covert means. Or, throwing himself under the protection of any two immediate kings of considerable power, he may defend himself against an immediate enemy. Or, having made an alliance with a chief in a stronghold, he may adopt double policy (i.e., make peace with one of the two kings, and wage war with another). Or, be may adapt himself to circumstances depending upon the causes of peace and war in order.

[AS-7.1.8] If any two kings hostile to each other find the time of achieving the results of their respective works to be equal, they shall make peace with each other.

[AS-10.3.20] Having broken the whole army (of the enemy), (the invader) should seek for peace; if the armies are of equal strength, he should make peace when requested for it; and if the enemy's army is inferior, he should attempt to destroy it, but not that which has secured a favourable position and is reckless of life.

question: office mein sab log politics karte hain, main kya karun
answer: Main yeh samjho ki politics band karne ki jagah apne kaam par focus karo—AS-1.8.8 ke hisaab se experience wale logon ki madad le, bas apne kaam ki quality par dhyan do. Aur AS-4.7.17 yaad rakho ki gussa sirf nuksaan laata hai, isse bachna aur solution dhundhna sahi hai. Aapka agla kadam kya hoga?
cited_verses:
[AS-1.8.8] "No," says the son of Báhudantí (a woman); "for a man possessed of only theoretical knowledge and having no experience of practical politics is likely to commit serious blunders when engaged in actual works. Hence he shall employ as ministers such as are born of high family and possessed of wisdom, purity of purpose, bravery and loyal feelings inasmuch as ministerial appointments shall purely depend on qualifications."

[AS-4.7.17] Offence to women or kinsmen, claiming inheritance, professional competition, hatred against rivals, commerce, guilds and any one of the legal disputes, is the cause of anger: anger is the cause of death.

question: What makes a treaty or an alliance worth entering?
answer: A treaty is worth entering when it brings genuine security and mutual benefit, not just temporary advantage. Look closely at whether the alliance strengthens your position without creating hidden dangers or dependence that could later be used against you, as warned in AS-9.5.1. Also consider if your ally remains reliable in crisis, not just when things are easy, reflecting the insight in AS-8.1.14 about trust being tested in hard times. What specific situation are you weighing where you need to judge an alliance’s true value?
cited_verses:
[AS-9.5.1] THE formation of a treaty and other settlements otherwise than they ought to have been made is impolicy. From it arise dangers.

[AS-8.1.14] No, says Kautilya, the ally of him who has a powerful army keeps the alliance; and even the enemy assumes a friendly attitude; when there is a work that can be equally accomplished either by the army or by an ally, then preference to the army or to the ally should depend on the advantages of securing the appropriate place and time for war and the expected profit. In times of sudden expedition and on occasions of troubles from an enemy, a wild tribe, or local rebels, no friend can be trusted. When calamities happen together, or when an enemy has grown strong, a friend keeps up his friendship as long as money is forthcoming. Thus the determination of the comparative seriousness of the calamities of the various elements of sovereignty.
note: AS-8.1.14 says no friend can be trusted in sudden troubles; answer presents it as "trust tested in hard times".

question: My manager takes credit for my work and plays politics
answer: Focus on delivering clear, valuable work that stands on its own, so your contributions are visible regardless of who speaks for them. AS-7.8.7 teaches that resolute effort without distraction builds genuine worth, while AS-1.19.7 warns that leaders who block access or take credit create confusion and distrust—signs to watch for in your environment. Keep doing your work well, document your contributions, and seek opportunities where your efforts are recognized directly. What’s one small way you could make your impact more visible this week?
cited_verses:
[AS-7.8.7] Whoever undertakes tolerable work is a beginner possible work: whoever undertakes an unblemished work is a beginner of praiseworthy work; whoever undertakes work of large profits is a beginner of a productive work; whoever takes no rest before the completion of the work undertaken is a resolute worker; and whoever has loyal and devoted subjects is in a position to command help and to bring to a successful termination any work without losing anything in the form of favour. When such friends are gratified by the enemy or the conqueror, they can be of immense help to him; friends of reverse character should never be helped.

[AS-1.19.7] When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.
note: AS-1.19.7 says nothing about taking credit; AS-7.8.7 is about resolute workers. Practical advice (document contributions) is good.

question: How do I care for my ageing parents without resenting them?
answer: Caring for ageing parents without resentment starts with seeing the duty as an act of inner strength, not just sacrifice. When you serve them with a steady mind, free from the pull of conflicting feelings like duty versus frustration, your action becomes a quiet offering. BG-7.28 reminds us that those free from the infatuation of opposing emotions act with firm resolve, and BG-13.9 points to letting go of sensory pride and understanding the shared reality of aging and sickness as a path forward. What small act of care can you do today that feels like a gift, not a burden?
cited_verses:
[BG-7.28] But those who act righteously, in whom sin has been destroyed, who are free from the infatuation of conflicting emotions, they worship Me with a firm resolve.

[BG-13.9] Renouncing the delights of the senses, being without pride, having a right understanding of the painful problem of birth and death, and of age and sickness;
note: Verses fit loosely; frames care as a gift but gives little practical help with resentment.

question: My boss micromanages every small thing I do
answer: You deserve to work without constant oversight when you’re capable. AS-1.19.7 reminds leaders that blocking access and over-controlling breeds confusion and disaffection—so your boss’s micromanaging may be hurting the team’s flow. AS-5.4.5 warns against secret talks and stubborn rigidity, which can mirror a boss who won’t let go of small tasks instead of trusting you. Try showing consistent results in one area first, then gently ask for space to own it fully. What’s one small task you could start managing independently this week?
cited_verses:
[AS-1.19.7] When in the court, he shall never cause his petitioners to wait at the door, for when a king makes himself inaccessible to his people and entrusts his work to his immediate officers, he may be sure to engender confusion in business, and to cause thereby public disaffection, and himself a prey to his enemies.

[AS-5.4.5] He shall also avoid talking to another in secret, mutual conversation with another in the assembly (of ministers), appearing in royal dress in the public, haughtiness, buffoonery, open request for gems and promotions, seeing with one eye, biting the lips, brow-beating, interrupting the king while speaking, enmity with a strong party, association with women, pimps, messengers of foreign kings, enemies, inimical parties, dismissed officers, and wicked people, stubborn adherence to a single purpose, and contact with any confederacy of men.
